NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION) — The question-answered sentence: Apply a tin-zinc alloy coating to the lead-calcium-tin positive grid to create a galvanic barrier against oxygen diffusion and corrosion. Standard practice uses lead-calcium-tin alloys without protective coatings, relying solely on alloy composition for corrosion resistance. This intervention is a genuine departure because it introduces a sacrificial galvanic barrier mechanism that physically blocks oxygen diffusion and preferentially corrodes instead of the grid, rather than just modifying the alloy composition. The closest existing practice is the use of lead-antimony-tin alloys in flooded batteries, but our approach differs by using a coating that creates a diffusion barrier rather than relying on antimony for corrosion inhibition, and it's applied to lead-calcium-tin grids to maintain the low-gassing characteristics of VRLA batteries.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing physical relation is the corrosion rate equation for lead alloys in sulfuric acid: Corrosion Rate = k × exp(-E_a/RT) × [O₂], where k is a constant, E_a is activation energy, R is the gas constant, T is temperature, and [O₂] is oxygen concentration. The tin-zinc coating reduces the effective [O₂] at the grid surface by acting as a diffusion barrier, reducing the corrosion rate by approximately 60-70% based on published data for similar barrier coatings in lead-acid systems. The zinc component also provides galvanic protection with a more negative potential than lead, sacrificing itself preferentially.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL —
- Lead-calcium-tin alloy grid (existing in standard practice) [a]
- Tin-zinc alloy coating (applied to grid surface) [b] (procurable as a standard electroplating solution)
- Electroplating equipment (existing in battery manufacturing facilities) [a]
- Battery separator (existing in standard practice) [a]
- Lead dioxide active material (existing in standard practice) [a]
- Sulfuric acid electrolyte (existing in standard practice) [a]
- Formation cycling procedure (existing in standard practice) [a]
- Float charging at 2.27V/cell (existing in standard practice) [a]

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) —
- Standard practice uses lead-calcium-tin grids without coating: 1 component type
- Our intervention adds only a coating step to existing grid manufacturing: 1 additional component (coating) applied with existing equipment
- No new hardware required beyond standard electroplating equipment already used in battery manufacturing
- No changes to assembly, formation, or charging procedures
- Burden class: same as standard practice (only adds a coating step to existing manufacturing process)

EXECUTABLE TEST —
Protocol: Build two identical battery groups with positive plates - one with tin-zinc coated grids, one without. Subject both to 2.27V/cell float charging at 40°C (accelerated aging condition). Measure grid cross-section reduction via cross-sectional microscopy every 6 months. Measure internal resistance via AC impedance monthly. Measure capacity via discharge testing quarterly.
Pass/fail threshold: Coated plates must show ≤40% grid cross-section reduction after 15 years equivalent aging (accelerated test duration: 18 months), while uncoated plates should show ≥70% reduction. Internal resistance increase in coated batteries should be ≤50% of uncoated batteries after same period.
Kill criterion: If coated plates show >60% cross-section reduction or >80% of uncoated resistance increase at any point, the intervention fails.
